Dynamical systems (xn+1​=F(xn​),x˙=f(x))

 Home Physics Branches of physics
OurBigBook.com Words: 30k Articles: 531
The study of dynamical systems asks how a state changes in time: which states persist, which orbits repeat, and how a small perturbation changes the future. A dynamical system combines a state space with an evolution rule. For a seasonal population, the state might be its abundance and one step one generation; for a harmonic oscillator, a state vector includes both position and velocity. Choosing a sufficient state is essential: position alone does not determine where an oscillator moves next.
The two basic descriptions are a discrete dynamical system, xn+1​=F(xn​), and an ordinary differential equation, x˙=f(x). Repeated iteration of a map gives xn​=Fn(x0​); an autonomous differential equation with unique solutions gives a flow map x(t)=Φt​(x0​). In either case, evolving for two successive durations agrees with evolving for their sum. The logistic map provides a particularly simple discrete dynamical system; the Lorenz system supplies a continuous-time example with a very different geometry.
Deterministic evolution says that the exact rule and exact initial condition specify one future. Predicting that future from measurements is a separate question. An instrument supplies a range of possible initial conditions, and a computation adds small errors. Near an asymptotically stable fixed point, nearby orbits converge and the long-term state can become easier to predict. With sensitive dependence on initial conditions, arbitrarily close starting states can eventually lead to a visible disagreement, even though each follows the same rule.
Much of the usefulness of dynamical systems comes from describing outcomes without writing every solution explicitly. Fixed points identify possible resting states; periodic orbits identify repeating behaviour; stability theory asks whether those behaviours survive small disturbances. A bifurcation diagram shows how changing a bifurcation parameter changes the possible outcomes. This is useful in population dynamics, where a stable abundance and an alternating abundance have different consequences, and in thermal convection, where a steady flow and a changing flow transport heat differently.
The beauty of the subject is that a small formula can organize a large variety of behaviour. The logistic map moves from an attracting fixed point to attracting periodic orbits and then to parameter values supporting sensitive motion. Its period-doubling cascade has a recognizable structure across many unimodal maps. Nevertheless, Devaney chaos, Glendinning chaos, and a positive Lyapunov exponent express different properties; a claim of chaos should specify its definition, its state space, and the parameter values under consideration.

Chaos

Words: 69
Dynamical systems OurBigBook.com
Chaos describes sustained irregular dynamics with sensitive dependence in a deterministic system. The precise convention matters. Devaney chaos requires topological transitivity, dense periodic orbits and sensitive dependence on an invariant set. A common operational flow description asks for bounded nonperiodic long-term motion with sensitive dependence. These formulations are useful in different settings and are not universally equivalent. A positive largest Lyapunov exponent is a numerical diagnostic of exponential separation, not by itself a proof of every topological definition.

Softening Rayleigh-Duffing oscillator (z′′+z=−Az′+z3−(z′)3)

Words: 148 Articles: 1
Dynamical systems OurBigBook.com
The softening restoring force and cubic velocity damping give the energy E=(z′)2/2+z2/2−z4/4 with E˙=−A(z′)2−(z′)4. The origin and the two saddle points z=±1 persist for all parameters. The origin undergoes a supercritical Hopf bifurcation at A=0. A heteroclinic cycle and a subsequent saddle-node bifurcation of periodic orbits are distinct global changes in its softening Rayleigh-Duffing phase portrait.

Softening Rayleigh-Duffing phase portrait

With a=−A>0, a stable cycle grows from the origin. At ah​≃0.33144619, symmetric saddle connections form a repelling heteroclinic cycle, while the stable inner cycle persists. Just above it an unstable outer cycle coexists with the stable one; they merge at af​≃0.33147066 in a saddle-node bifurcation of periodic orbits. These approximate values follow from the half-return equations Ha​(p)=p, with Ha′​(p)=1 at the fold, and saddle-manifold shooting at the connection. A coarse parameter scan can miss the narrow coexistence interval. The saddle eigenvalue ratio is below one at the connection, proving that the loop is repelling and preventing identification of the stable cycle's disappearance with that connection.

Attractor

Dynamical systems OurBigBook.com
An invariant set approached by trajectories from a neighborhood in the state space of a dynamical system. An attracting equilibrium point and an attracting limit cycle are elementary examples. In more precise definitions, compactness and an appropriate stability or trapping condition are often also required.

Attraction in a dynamical system

Words: 27
Attractor OurBigBook.com
Attraction in a dynamical system means convergence of nearby forward trajectories toward a specified invariant state or set. Attraction and Lyapunov stability are separate properties; together they give the usual local asymptotic stability of an equilibrium.

Under the geometric convention, a strange attractor is an attracting invariant set with irregular, typically fractal geometry rather than a smooth point, cycle or torus. Geometry and orbit instability are separate properties. A strange nonchaotic attractor can be geometrically strange without positive exponential separation. Some authors build chaos into the term instead, so that convention must be distinguished when using it.

Quasiperiodically forced systems provide primary examples in which strangeness and a positive largest Lyapunov exponent do not coincide. Consequently a fractal-looking numerical plot alone cannot establish chaos. [ref]

Hyperbolic invariant set

Words: 75
Dynamical systems OurBigBook.com
A compact invariant set K of a smooth invertible map f is uniformly hyperbolic when its tangent spaces split continuously as Es⊕Eu, the derivative preserves this splitting, and constants C>0, 0<ρ<1 satisfy ∥Dfnvs​∥≤Cρn∥vs​∥ and ∥Df−nvu​∥≤Cρn∥vu​∥ for every n≥0. Thus the stable direction contracts forward and the unstable direction contracts backward. A Smale horseshoe is an example with nontrivial symbolic dynamics; such a set can contain infinitely many saddle periodic orbits without attracting an open neighborhood.

Smale horseshoe

Words: 87
Dynamical systems OurBigBook.com
A Smale horseshoe is a compact hyperbolic invariant set of a smooth map with expanding and contracting directions and at least two strips that stretch across a common rectangle. Iterating the strips and their inverse images produces a Cantor-set product on which the dynamics are conjugate to a full shift. It supplies infinitely many saddle periodic orbits and chaotic itineraries; hyperbolicity alone does not make it an attracting invariant set. The geometric construction explains why phase-dependent reinjection near a Shilnikov bifurcation can create chaos even when the associated symmetric amplitude equations have no such mechanism.

Dynamical systems OurBigBook.com
An equivariant dynamical system has a vector field commuting with the action of a symmetry group. Its flow map preserves every subgroup's fixed-point subspace, because equivariance and uniqueness keep initial states fixed by that subgroup. Polynomial normal forms are constrained by the weights and parity of the group representation.

For four amplitudes whose wavevectors span a plane, this leaves two independent phase variables after quotienting translations. At zero amplitude, polar phases are undefined, so smooth centre manifold equations should first be written in Cartesian amplitudes.

Thus an integer vector d=p−q contributes at degree N exactly when the wavevector equation holds, ∥d∥1​≤N, and N−∥d∥1​ is even. The extra even degree is supplied by factors ∣Aj​∣2. This finite integer test distinguishes regular saturation terms from phase-sensitive resonance terms.

The statement guarantees existence and symmetry type, not stability or which parameter side contains every branch.

For odd dihedral groups the reflection normalizer has no such quotient; an even-degree anisotropic term can distinguish the two half-axes at higher order.

Relative equilibrium

Words: 160 Articles: 1
Dynamical systems OurBigBook.com
A relative equilibrium is a solution that is stationary after undoing motion generated by a continuous symmetry. For complex amplitudes with a common rotation symmetry, constant moduli and constant relative phases can accompany a common phase evolving at constant frequency. Quotienting by the symmetry turns that solution into an ordinary equilibrium.

Relative equilibrium OurBigBook.com
For identical point vortices on the plane, use ω=∑a​dxa​∧dya​, ιXH​​ω=dH, and L=21​∑a​(xa2​+ya2​). The generator Y of simultaneous counterclockwise rotations is −XL​, and L is its moment map with the convention ιY​ω=−dL. In coordinates rotating with angular velocity Ω, the Hamiltonian vector field is XH​−ΩY=XH+ΩL​. Hence a collision-free configuration rigidly rotating at that velocity is exactly a critical point of the augmented Hamiltonian function H+ΩL. For H=−∑a<b​log∣ra​−rb​∣2, scaling all positions shows ∑a​ra​⋅∇a​H=−N(N−1); a rotating relative equilibrium therefore obeys 2ΩL=N(N−1). For N≥2 this implies positive Ω in the stated circulation convention. Reversing the contraction convention requires consistent changes to the Hamiltonian and rotation signs.

Unstable manifold (Wu)

Words: 59
Dynamical systems OurBigBook.com
At a hyperbolic equilibrium, the unstable manifold is formed by nearby trajectories approaching that equilibrium as time tends to minus infinity. It is tangent to the span of eigenvectors whose eigenvalues have positive real part. Its dimension counts departing amplitudes; translation along an autonomous trajectory can remove one parameter when comparing orbit shapes. The stable manifold instead approaches the equilibrium forward in time.

A heteroclinic cycle is a closed chain of invariant states connected by heteroclinic orbits. In convection-amplitude models it can describe successive convection roll switching. Phase locking is the maintenance of a fixed phase relation (possibly an integer combination of phases) between coupled oscillations, or between a pattern and imposed forcing. The following spatial-forcing example occurs in an amplitude equation. For a real-coefficient conjugately forced amplitude equation, A=ρeiϕ obeys ρT​=(μ+βcos2ϕ−λρ2)ρ and ϕT​=−βsin2ϕ. Thus forcing selects stable phases 0,π for β>0 and π/2,3π/2 for β<0, when a nonzero amplitude exists. At β=0 this pinning disappears and the phase is neutral.

Topological dynamics studies continuous maps and their orbits on topological spaces. For a compact metric space X and a continuous map T:X→X, the pair (X,T) is a compact Hausdorff topological dynamical system.

A continuous map on a nonempty topological space is point-transitive if it has a dense forward orbit. This is one convention for topological transitivity, but on spaces with isolated points it must be distinguished from the open-set intersection definition. On a nonempty compact metric space, the positive-time open-set intersection property implies point transitivity: for each member Uj​ of a countable basis of a topology, ⋃n≥1​f−n(Uj​) is open and dense, and the Baire category theorem supplies a point in their intersection. Conversely, a surjective point-transitive continuous map has every tail of its dense orbit dense, since fk(X)=X and continuity sends its orbit closure into the closure of that tail. The map f(1/j)=1/(j+1), f(0)=0 on {0}∪{1/j:j≥1} is point-transitive but fails the open-set intersection property.

Every continuous self-map of a nonempty compact metric space has a recurrent point. Choose a minimal subsystem. The forward orbit of every point in it is dense, and the same is true of every tail of that orbit; consequently each neighborhood is revisited at arbitrarily large times. A nonempty subsystem is all that is guaranteed: the identity map on a singleton has no larger subsystem.

infn≥0​d(Tnx,Tny)=0.
(1)

Asymptotic-pair obstruction to an invariant metric

Words: 68
Proximality OurBigBook.com
If distinct points x,y of a dynamical system on a compact metric space satisfy d(Tnx,Tny)→0 in one compatible metric, no compatible metric can make T an isometry. On a compact space, all compatible metrics give the same asymptotic-pair property by uniform continuity, whereas an isometry preserves the strictly positive distance between distinct points. In a full shift, a constant sequence and a sequence differing at just one coordinate converge to each other under forward shifts, proving this obstruction directly in the product topology.

Joint return lemma for a proximal minimal pair

Words: 122
Proximality OurBigBook.com
For a compact metric space with a continuous map T, suppose y is a minimal point and x,y are proximal. Every neighborhood U of y admits arbitrarily large n with Tnx,Tny∈U. First shrink U to an open neighborhood, then choose an open V with y∈V and V⊆U. Minimality and compactness give a finite cover of the orbit closure of y by T−jV, 0≤j≤J. Uniform continuity of these finitely many iterates turns a sufficiently close proximal encounter into a common visit to U after at most J more steps. If the proximal encounters occur only at bounded times, a zero distance at some time makes the two future orbits coincide, and minimality then gives arbitrarily late common visits. Thus injectivity is not needed for this general lemma.

A nonempty topological dynamical system (Y,T) on a compact Hausdorff space is minimal if it has no proper nonempty closed forward-invariant subset. Equivalently, every forward orbit is dense in Y, because an orbit closure is closed and forward invariant. Minimality implies T(Y)=Y.

A two-sided sequence over a finite alphabet is uniformly recurrent if every finite word over an alphabet occurring in it occurs with bounded gaps. This is equivalent to being a minimal point of the full shift: a finite cover of the orbit closure by preimages of a word's cylinder set bounds its return gaps; conversely, bounded gaps pass to all points of the orbit closure and make every forward orbit dense there. The property concerns finite words, not infinite integer intervals.

Dynamical system OurBigBook.com
Evolution is deterministic when a specified initial condition and evolution rule select a unique future orbit. For a discrete dynamical system, applying the same map to the same state gives the same next state. For p=2/3, the nonboundary alternating sequence has even-level log ratio (n/2)log(8/9), which tends to −∞. The geometric Gibbs law is the special case p=1/2.

Butterfly effect

Words: 676 Articles: 1
Devaney chaos OurBigBook.com
The butterfly effect is the intuitive idea that an arbitrarily small change in an initial condition can eventually change the observed future substantially. In dynamical systems, sensitive dependence makes this precise for a map F:X→X on a metric space (X,d): there is one separation scale δ>0 such that
∀x∈X ∀ε>0 ∃y∈X ∃n≥0:d(x,y)<ε,d(Fn(x),Fn(y))>δ.
(27)
The same δ works at every point, whereas y and the separation time n may depend on the point and the requested closeness. For a flow map, replace the iteration of a map Fn by Φt​ with some t≥0. The state space matters: restricting to a single fixed point removes the alternative nearby states needed for sensitivity.
Sensitivity is compatible with deterministic evolution. Given an exact initial condition, there is still one orbit; uncertainty concerns which exact state a measurement represents. It also allows accurate short-term prediction. For a continuous function F, each fixed finite iterated function Fn is continuous, so sufficiently close initial states remain close at any specified finite step. What fails is a single initial accuracy that controls every future step.
The logistic map illustrates both sides. At r=2.8, nearby orbits in the basin of attraction of its attracting fixed point approach one another. At r=4, arbitrarily close states can eventually separate by a macroscopic fraction of [0,1]. The definition asserts the existence of separating neighbours, not that every nearby pair must separate: x and 1−x have exactly the same next state under the logistic map and hence the same subsequent orbit. Nor must separation increase at every step.
A positive Lyapunov exponent describes average exponential growth of an infinitesimal displacement along an orbit, when the relevant limit exists. It is related to sensitivity but is not a substitute for its uniform definition. For a differentiable interval map, the chain rule gives
λ(x0​)=limN→∞​N1​∑j=0N−1​log∣F′(xj​)∣.
(28)
At r=4, the logistic map has λ=log2 for Lebesgue measure-almost every initial condition, while exceptional orbits can have different exponents. Finite-separation growth is only approximately exponential while the linear approximation remains useful. In a bounded state space, a separation cannot grow exponentially forever.
Sensitivity alone is also weaker than Devaney chaos, which additionally requires topological transitivity and dense periodic points. For example, F(x)=2x on the real line has sensitive dependence and a positive Lyapunov exponent, but its only periodic point is zero, so it is not Devaney-chaotic. This distinguishes growth of uncertainty from the richer organization of recurrent orbits.
Edward N. Lorenz's "Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow" (1963) studied a thermal convection model with three ordinary differential equations. Its numerical orbits exhibited persistent nonperiodic motion and instability to small changes of the initial condition. Lorenz discussed the consequences for very-long-range weather forecasting: a deterministic law need not make a detailed distant future reliably recoverable from approximate observations. The historically relevant lesson of the Lorenz system is this growth of uncertainty under deterministic evolution.[ref]

Even a bounded linearization leaves nonlinear stability undecided. The two displayed maps of the complex plane have the same derivative, a rotation matrix. Their radial updates are r↦r(1−r2) and r↦r(1+r2). For small positive radius, the first decreases to zero and the second moves out of every sufficiently small fixed neighborhood. Hyperbolic equilibrium point OurBigBook.com
For a continuously differentiable dynamical system x˙=f(x), a fixed point is hyperbolic if no eigenvalue of its Jacobian has zero real part. In a neighborhood of a hyperbolic fixed point, the nonlinear flow is locally topologically conjugate to its linearized flow. Thus the saddle, attracting or repelling character persists under the nonlinear terms. The theorem does not decide the nonlinear character of an equilibrium with purely imaginary or zero eigenvalues: a conserved Hamiltonian, Lyapunov function or higher-order analysis may be needed instead.

Two real eigenvalues with opposite signs give a saddle equilibrium; all real parts positive give a source. Purely imaginary or zero eigenvalues require a separate nonlinear analysis. Merely having distinct eigenvalues does not remove this exception.

A weak focus is an isolated planar equilibrium point with nonzero imaginary eigenvalues and nearby trajectories that spiral toward or away from it because of nonlinear terms. For example, if the radial return map is P(r)=r+κr2m+1+O(r2m+2) with κ=0, sufficiently small positive r decreases under successive returns when κ<0 and increases when κ>0. The first case gives asymptotic stability; the second gives instability. Equivalently, if a positive local function W=r2+O(r3) satisfies W˙=cr2m+2+O(r2m+3) and the angular velocity stays positive, then the sign of c settles the same question. A quadratic planar system can have its cubic radial drift vanish and still have a nonzero fifth-order radial drift.

This real planar dynamical system has a saddle point at (−1,0) and a repelling weak focus at (1,0). The latter has purely imaginary linearized eigenvalues ±2i, so its linearization has closed elliptical orbits. Nonlinear terms nevertheless produce outward drift.
Set X=2(x−1), Y=y, τ=2t and r2=X2+Y2. The cubic expansion is
Xτ​=Y+Y2+21​XY2+21​Y3+O(r4),Yτ​=−X−43​X2−21​Y2−41​X3+O(r4).
(48)
The linear rotation acts on scalar functions by L=Y∂X​−X∂Y​. For H2​=r2/2, its cubic derivative is XY2−3X2Y/4−Y3/2. The homogeneous correction H3​=7X3/12+XY2/2+Y3/3 satisfies LH3​ equal to the negative of that derivative. The remaining quartic derivative of H2​+H3​ is 3X2Y2/2−X3Y. With
H4​=41​X4−163​X3Y+163​XY3,
(49)
direct differentiation gives
dτd​(H2​+H3​+H4​)=163​r4+O(r5)>0
(50)
for all sufficiently small nonzero r. Meanwhile H2​+H3​+H4​=r2/2+O(r3)>0. In reversed time it is a strict Lyapunov function, proving asymptotic stability of the reversed system and hence repulsion forward in time. The angular speed stays close to −1, so the nearby nonzero trajectories spiral rather than approaching along a fixed direction. This explicit calculation illustrates why a centre in the linearization need not be a nonlinear centre.

Quartic Lyapunov correction for a weak focus (V=21​r2+V4​,V˙=κr4+O(r6))

Words: 159
Weak focus OurBigBook.com
Consider a smooth planar system x˙=y+P3​(x,y)+O(r5), y˙​=−x+Q3​(x,y)+O(r5), where P3​,Q3​ are homogeneous cubic polynomials and r2=x2+y2. The leading derivative of r2/2 is the quartic polynomial H4​=xP3​+yQ3​. Let κ be the angular average of H4​ on the unit circle. A homogeneous quartic correction V4​ solving
(y∂x​−x∂y​)V4​=κr4−H4​
(51)
gives V˙=κr4+O(r6) for V=r2/2+V4​. The right side has zero angular average. Since y∂x​−x∂y​=−∂θ​, its nonconstant angular Fourier modes can be integrated individually to obtain a periodic quartic correction; only modes of orders two and four can occur after removing the constant average.
The correction is O(r4), so V remains positive definite close to zero. If κ<0, its orbital derivative is strictly negative there, and the Second Lyapunov theorem proves asymptotic stability. If κ>0, apply the same argument in reversed time to obtain repulsion. If κ=0, this quartic calculation alone does not decide stability. This method converts the averaged damping of a weak focus into a pointwise sign for a Lyapunov function.

Positively invariant set

Words: 76 Articles: 1
Dynamical systems OurBigBook.com
A set is positively invariant when every forward trajectory starting in it remains in it.
This is a dynamical example of an invariant; forward invariance and strict inward trapping are additional conditions.

Trapping region

Words: 44
Positively invariant set OurBigBook.com
A trapping region is a compact region across whose boundary the vector field points inward. It is positively invariant and confines every forward trajectory that enters it.
This is a dynamical example of an invariant; forward invariance and strict inward trapping are additional conditions.

Steady state

Words: 29
Dynamical systems OurBigBook.com
A steady state is a state whose observable description is independent of time. In a transport problem it can sustain nonzero fluxes even though local fields remain time independent.
